title: Estimate and Check
context: Grade 4, the closing topic, and it answers the question the opening page asked, which wanted an approximate number rather than an exact one. An adult sees rounding done twice and then added. What the page is actually doing is putting an estimate to work: it is not a worse answer, it is a fast one, and its job is to tell you whether the exact answer you worked out is anywhere near right.

writeup.why: Get a quick answer by rounding the numbers first, then use it to decide whether the exact answer you worked out is sensible.
writeup.look: A stage split down the middle, the exact sum building in columns on one side and the rounded sum on the other, with a bar between the answers.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Estimate and Check' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many addends have been rounded against how many there are, two numbers side by side in ink, and under them the unit the question named, written in words rather than in figures; on the last two phases it carries the two answers, the estimated one in rose above the exact one in green. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The working area is split down the middle at x 607 by one ruled line that runs its whole height, and the two sides never borrow each other's room. The unit picker runs along the top, three keys 180 by 52 at 64,202, at 258,202 and at 452,202, reading nearest hundred, nearest thousand and nearest ten thousand, with the chosen one standing proud of the other two; on the first phase it is already set and locked, because the unit comes out of the question, and on the second the two keys the question offers are both live. The exact side is 520 by 300 at 64,266: a heading row 34 tall of six ruled cells reading L, TTh, Th, H, T and O, a carry strip 32 tall above it where a carried digit stands small and vermilion over the column it is being added into, the addend rows in deep blue, a rule 4 tall under the last addend and the sum row in green. The estimate side is the same rectangle at 630,266 with no columns drawn in it at all, which is the point of it: the rounded addends are printed large in rose one under another with their trailing zeros in grey, a rule is drawn under the last of them, and the estimated sum stands in rose under the rule. A number line strip 470 by 56 runs under each rounded addend, zoomed so that the two nearest multiples of the chosen unit sit at its ends on label plates, with a halfway tick 4 by 40 standing between them and its value printed above it, and a drawn pin marking the addend where it belongs on the line; the shorter of the two distances from the pin fills amber the moment both are drawn, so the nearer end is seen before a single digit is read. The gap bar is 1086 by 76 at 64,578, drawn only when both sums are standing: it runs from the exact sum to the estimated sum, touching each, with how far apart they are printed at its middle, and it is drawn in ink rather than in either answer's colour so that neither answer owns it. The check bay is 1086 by 68 at 64,662, a slot 420 wide at its left holding an answer somebody else has written, room beside it for the estimate to build, and two keys at its right reading could be right and go back and check; the bay never marks the written answer, it draws the bar and asks which of the two the child would work again. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across, with a thirteenth key that writes a run of zeros so a rounded addend or an estimated sum can be finished in one press. On the second phase a strip of three unit words, hundred, thousand and ten thousand, sits under the keys, because an estimate is given with its unit named or it is not given at all. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, a carried digit is vermilion and always drawn small above the column it is being added into, a rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, the digit under discussion or the one that is missing is amber, and a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, and a carry is told by being small and sitting above the rule.
writeup.finish: The card shows one pair estimated and added exactly, side by side, with the gap between the two answers still drawn.

phases.win: the estimate lands without a single column being written
phases.does: rounds both addends and adds the rounded numbers
phases.goal: the rounding happens first and the adding happens to the rounded numbers
phases.says: Round each number first, then add. Not the other way round.
phases.check: Estimate those two crowds to the nearest thousand. Which did you do first, the rounding or the adding?
phases.feels: the adding turns out to be the easy half, and all of the work is in the rounding that comes first
phases.hands: Write the two addends on paper, cross out the digits standing to the right of the rounding place in each one and write the rounded number underneath it, and only then draw the plus sign and add.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of your two numbers is already rounded? Second rung, the phase's: which two round numbers is the other one sitting between? Third rung: the estimate side is cut to one addend and its strip, and that number is rounded on its own before the other comes back. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: rounding the answer is one rounding instead of two, and the answer is the thing the question seems to be about.
wrong.move: adds the two addends exactly and rounds the answer afterwards, handing that in as the estimate.
wrong.screen: the two roads are drawn side by side on the estimate side with the order of their steps numbered beside them: rounding the two crowds of 23,501 and 32,546 to the nearest thousand first gives 24,000 and 33,000, which come to 57,000, while adding first gives 56,047 and rounding that afterwards gives 56,000. Both are printed, neither is crossed out, and the question's own wording is lit above them.

wrong.why: the first number was the one being worked on, and the second looked ready to use just as it was.
wrong.move: rounds one addend, leaves the other exactly as it stands and adds the two together.
wrong.screen: the number line strip opens under the addend that was left alone, with the two nearest multiples of the unit on plates at its ends and the pin standing between them; the estimate side takes rounded numbers only, so that addend waits out on its strip until it is sent to one end or the other. Nothing already written is cleared.

phases.screen: two addends with the estimate side empty and the unit already set
phases.soWhat: Round every addend first and then add the rounded numbers, which needs no columns at all because they end in zeros.

phases.win: two different estimates stand together and neither is crossed out
phases.does: estimates the pair to one unit, then to the other, and compares
phases.goal: the unit comes from the question, and a different unit gives a different estimate
phases.says: Read the question again. Which unit is it asking for?
phases.check: Estimate this pair to the nearest hundred, then to the nearest thousand. Why are both answers right?
phases.feels: one pair of numbers and two different estimates, and both of them survive
phases.hands: Round the same pair of numbers to the nearest hundred on one line and to the nearest thousand on the line underneath, and read the two estimates straight down the page.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what unit does the question name? Second rung, the phase's: which two numbers of that size is your addend between? Third rung: the unit picker is cut to the one key the question names and both strips rezoom to match it. The unit words stay open under the pad.

wrong.why: rounding is the job that was asked for, and one round number looks about as useful as another.
wrong.move: rounds to whichever unit makes the numbers easiest, without reading the unit out of the question.
wrong.screen: the question is reprinted across the top with its unit underlined, and the estimate side builds twice, once under each unit, the two estimates standing one above the other with the unit each was rounded to named under it. Neither is crossed out and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: two different answers to one question have meant a mistake every time so far.
wrong.move: says the estimate made under the other unit must be wrong, because it does not match the one just made.
wrong.screen: two strips open together under the same addend, one zoomed to the hundreds either side of it and one to the thousands either side, with the same pin standing on both; the nearer end is a different number on each strip, and on each strip it really is the nearer end. Nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the same pair with the unit picker offering the nearest hundred and the nearest thousand
phases.soWhat: The unit is set by the question, so read it before rounding anything and say it whenever you give an estimate.

phases.win: the gap bar is drawn short and labelled, and both answers stay standing
phases.does: runs the gap bar and reads how far apart the two answers are
phases.goal: the estimate is near the exact sum rather than equal to it
phases.says: Put the estimate next to the exact answer. How far apart are they?
phases.check: Your estimate is 90,000 and your exact answer is 88,984. Is your estimate wrong?
phases.feels: near is good enough, and near was what the question asked for all along
phases.hands: Work the sum exactly on the left of a page and estimate it on the right, then rule a line between the two answers and write on that line how far apart they are.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: were you asked for an exact sum or a quick one? Second rung, the phase's: how far apart are your two answers? Third rung: the gap bar is laid against the length of the exact sum, so the distance is read against the size of the number it belongs to. Both answers stay on the stage.

wrong.why: an answer that does not match the right answer has been a wrong answer every time until now.
wrong.move: calls the estimate wrong because it does not equal the exact sum.
wrong.screen: the two answers drop onto one number line together, the exact sum of 88,984 and the estimated sum of 90,000 that the pair 42,135 and 46,849 gives, and the space between them is drawn and labelled; the line runs the whole length of the sum, so the gap is seen against what was being measured rather than on its own. Both answers stay standing.

wrong.why: an exact answer is the better answer, and the estimate side looks like a slower way to the same place.
wrong.move: rounds the addends and then writes the exact sum into the estimate's place, because the exact sum is the one they trust.
wrong.screen: the estimate side shows that it has no columns to clear away and adds its two rounded numbers straight across in one line, while the exact side keeps its six ruled columns with its carried digit still standing small above the column it joined. The two ways of arriving at an answer are left side by side with the work each one took still showing.

phases.screen: both sides finished with the gap bar waiting between them
phases.soWhat: An estimate is meant to land near the exact sum rather than equal it, and the gap stays small because each addend only moved a little.
phases.concept: An estimate sits close to the exact answer

phases.win: the gap bar stretches long and the written answer is sent back to be worked again
phases.does: builds the estimate and decides whether the written answer can be right
phases.goal: an answer far from its estimate is the one to go back to
phases.says: Your estimate and your answer are far apart. Which would you check first?
phases.check: You added two numbers and got an answer far below your estimate. What do you do next, and why not simply add it again?
phases.feels: a fast answer that is roughly right catches an exact answer that is badly wrong
phases.hands: Before working a sum out at all, estimate it in your head and write that estimate in the margin, then work the sum properly and read the margin back.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does your estimate say the answer should be near? Second rung, the phase's: how far from it is the answer standing in the bay? Third rung: the written sum is lit one column at a time from the ones until the first column that disagrees is found. Nothing in the bay is ever marked right or wrong.

wrong.why: a sum that is set out tidily looks like a sum that has gone well.
wrong.move: trusts a written answer because its columns look neat, and never builds the estimate beside it.
wrong.screen: the estimate builds in a moment on the right, 28,450 going to 30,000 and 31,260 going to 30,000 for an estimate of 60,000, and the gap bar is run from there to the written answer of 5,971; the bar stretches right across the stage with how far apart they are printed on it, and the written sum is left standing exactly as it was with all its columns still showing.

wrong.why: a wrong answer feels like work to be thrown away rather than work to be looked at.
wrong.move: sees the gap stretch long and rubs the whole sum out to begin it again.
wrong.screen: the columns of the written sum light one at a time from the ones, and the first column whose digit does not agree with the rebuilt one is the only one left lit; the rest of the sum stays standing, and the gap bar shortens as that single column is put right. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the check bay holding a written answer with the estimate building beside it
phases.soWhat: An answer far from its estimate is the one to go back to, and building the estimate to find that out costs almost nothing.
phases.concept: An estimate is how you check an exact answer

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the gap bar is run. The two answers lift off their own sides of the stage and come down together onto one long line drawn from nothing up to the exact sum, and the distance between them, which read as a whole number of its own a moment ago, turns out to be no wider on that line than the pin that marks it. The printed label stays beside the gap, so the number that measures it and the size of it are both on the stage at once, and they do not look like the same thing at all. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the two addends stand in deep blue down the exact side with its columns ruled and its sum row empty, the estimate side is blank, the unit picker along the top is already set to the unit the question named and will not move, and a number line strip is drawn under each addend but not yet zoomed. On the second the same pair stands there with two of the unit keys proud, either of which may be pressed. On the third both sides are finished, the exact sum in green and the estimated sum in rose, and the gap bar lies between them drawn and unlabelled. On the fourth the check bay is open along the foot with somebody else's answer already in its slot and the estimate side empty beside it. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the number line strip under the first addend, or the unit key, or the empty label on the gap bar, gives one slow pulse while the voice says to round the numbers first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any addends, any unit, with both sides running, the number line strips open and the gap bar live. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on rounding the addends first, rounding to the unit that was asked for, and using an estimate to check.

observations.why: Rounded numbers end in zeros, and zeros carry nothing into anything.
observations.soWhat: An estimate is quick, and being quick is the whole reason for having one.
observations.observe: The estimate landed without one column being written on that side of the stage.

observations.why: The unit decides which two round numbers an addend is sitting between.

observations.observe: The same pair gave a different estimate under each unit and neither was crossed out.

observations.why: Both addends moved a little on their way to being round, and the estimate carries those moves in it.
observations.soWhat: Close was the job. Equal was never the job.

source_tool.description: The stage is split down the middle. On the left the addends are added exactly, in columns, the way the rest of the chapter does it. On the right the same addends are rounded first and the rounded numbers are added, which takes no columns at all because they end in zeros. A unit picker at the top says which unit the rounding is to, and it is set by the question rather than by the child: changing it re-rounds both addends and rebuilds the estimate, so the same pair can be seen giving different estimates for different units, all of them right for the unit they were asked for. A number line strip under each addend shows it sitting between the two nearest multiples of the chosen unit, so rounding stays a choice of the nearer rather than a rule about a digit. When both sides are finished, a gap bar is drawn between the estimated sum and the exact sum and labelled with how far apart they are. A check bay takes an answer somebody else has written, builds the estimate beside it and asks whether the written answer is anywhere near.
source_tool.art_direction: A split stage, exact sum and estimate / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that tie themselves together, a rule under the last addend, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A sum is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the addends stacked with their right ends aligned, and a horizontal rule between the last addend and the sum. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach adding.
A carried digit is always drawn small, above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, and a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, so an estimate is told apart from an exact answer before either is read. The digit under discussion, which is usually the one that is missing, is amber. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carry is told apart by being small and sitting above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

placement.where: After one pair has been estimated on paper and the exact sum worked beside it. The tool is what keeps both answers up at once and measures the gap, which a written page can only do by being read twice.

answer_key.rule: To estimate a sum, round every addend to the unit the question names and then add the rounded numbers. The unit comes from the question, so the same pair of addends gives different estimates for different units and each is right for the unit it was asked for. An estimate is not meant to equal the exact sum, only to land near it. If the exact answer and the estimate are far apart, one of the two is wrong and both are worth checking.
answer_key.wrong: The number line strip reopens under each addend with the two nearest multiples of the chosen unit at its ends, so the nearer one can be seen before the rule is read. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Round 3,780 to the nearest thousand, which gives 4,000.
Round 4,150 to the nearest thousand, which gives 4,000.
Add the rounded numbers: 4,000 + 4,000 = 8,000, and the exact sum of 7,930 is close to it.
items.question: Estimate 3,780 + 4,150 by rounding each addend to the nearest thousand.
items.checkpoint: Rounding comes first and the adding is done to the rounded numbers.
items.misconception: Adding first and rounding the answer afterwards, which is a different question from the one asked.

steps: To the nearest hundred, 2,640 becomes 2,600 and 5,180 becomes 5,200, which add to 7,800.
To the nearest thousand, 2,640 becomes 3,000 and 5,180 becomes 5,000, which add to 8,000.
Both are right for the unit they were asked for, and the exact sum is 7,820.
items.answer: 7,800 to the nearest hundred, and 8,000 to the nearest thousand
items.question: Estimate 2,640 + 5,180 to the nearest hundred, and then to the nearest thousand.
items.checkpoint: The unit is set by the question, and a different unit gives a different estimate.
items.misconception: Rounding to the nearest thousand when the question asked for the nearest hundred.

steps: Round each addend to the nearest ten thousand: 42,860 gives 40,000 and 37,410 gives 40,000.
The exact sum is 80,270, so the estimate lands near it without matching it.
items.answer: The estimate is 80,000 and the exact sum is 80,270, which is close to it
items.question: Estimate 42,860 + 37,410 by rounding each addend to the nearest ten thousand, and compare it with the exact sum.
items.checkpoint: An estimate is meant to land near the exact sum, not to equal it.
items.misconception: Calling the estimate wrong because it does not come to 80,270.

steps: Round the addends: 28,450 gives 30,000 and 31,260 gives 30,000.
5,971 is far below that, so the working has gone wrong somewhere, and adding the columns properly gives 59,710.
items.answer: The estimate is 60,000 and 5,971 is nowhere near it, so the answer is wrong. The sum is 59,710
items.question: A child added 28,450 and 31,260 and wrote 5,971. Use an estimate to the nearest ten thousand to check it.
items.checkpoint: An answer far from its estimate is an answer to go back to.
items.misconception: Trusting a written answer because the columns look neat, instead of standing an estimate beside it.

teaching_notes: Round first and add second, every time, and say it in that order out loud, because adding first and rounding the answer is a different question that gives a different number. Read the unit out of the question before anything is rounded. The printed exercises name the nearest hundred in one place and the nearest thousand in another, and a child who rounds to whichever unit they like will be right about the method and wrong about the answer. Build the teaching on the worked example that adds 42,135 and 46,849: rounded to the nearest ten thousand those become 40,000 and 50,000, so the estimated sum is 90,000 against an actual sum of 88,984, and the two standing side by side are exactly the point. Read the two crowd figures beside the estimating heading as rounded to the nearest thousand, which is what the numbers printed next to them are; rounding either of them to the nearest ten thousand would give 40,000, so do not run that pair as a ten thousands example. Finish on the check bay. An estimate that is never used to check anything has not yet done its job, and this is where the opening question about approximately how many trains run daily is finally answered.
generation_prompt: Build an estimating tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage split down the middle. On the left the addends are added exactly in a ruled column mat with carries drawn in circles. On the right the same addends are rounded first and the rounded numbers are added with no columns at all. A unit picker across the top selects the nearest hundred, thousand or ten thousand and re-rounds both addends live, rebuilding the estimate so the same pair can be seen giving different estimates for different units, none of them crossed out. A number line strip under each addend zooms so that the two nearest multiples of the chosen unit sit at its ends, with the addend marked between them. When both sides are finished, a gap bar is drawn between the estimated sum and the exact sum and labelled with the distance between them. A check bay accepts an answer typed in from elsewhere, builds the estimate beside it and stretches the gap bar long when the two are far apart. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read which unit the question asks for and set the picker to it. Round both numbers first, then add the rounded ones. Work the exact sum on the other side and run the gap bar between the two answers. If they are far apart, go back and check your working.
